title: Field hotswap requests and cost tradeoffs — sprint snapshot
content:
Purpose:
This is a working snapshot of field-originated hotswap requests (customers asking for runtime model or config swaps mid-flight), plus our distilled heuristics for when to approve, recommend, or block them based on cost/latency/regression risk. Goal is a concise playbook we can use when triaging incoming asks this sprint and a short list of low-effort mitigations the SRE/Runtime teams can prototype next week.

Context / why this matters:
- Several enterprise customers toggled model variants during heavy traffic windows in August and reported both sudden token-cost spikes and subtle quality regressions.
- The ops burden to revert or investigate mid-window increases MTTR and causes customer-facing SLA implications.
- Customers repeatedly ask for a quick knob to move between cheaper quantized variants and higher-quality variants depending on workload.

Raw asks heard (field snippets):
- "Can we switch to 4bit-quant for nightly batch jobs to save tokens, then swap back for daytime low-latency queries?" (Finance app, mid-market)
- "When our prompt distribution spikes longer tail sequences, the p50 latency is fine but p99 rockets. We want an automated fallback to a lower-context model during peak traffic." (Marketplace search)
- "We need a way to test model variants in prod without creating duplicate routes — simple toggle please." (SaaS search vendor)

Observed pain patterns and impact metrics (from logs + CS notes):
- Quick swaps increased token cost by ~15–40% for customers that moved from Q4 small to Q8 medium due to unanticipated output length changes (sampled across 8 accounts).
- Kv-cache fragmentation: frequent variant changes caused cache warm-up penalties, raising p95 generation latency by ~120ms on average in first 5 minutes after switch.
- Rollback churn: manual rollback took 18–72 minutes depending on traceability; customers penalized for failures.

Heuristic triage matrix (draft):
- Low risk: internal scheduled batch -> allow swap if expected cost reduction >10% and no short-tail latency requirement. Approve via self-serve UI with confirmation and rollback window.
- Medium risk: public-facing synchronous route with <200ms p95 target -> recommend canary on subset (5–10%) with auto-fallback if latency/regression thresholds breached.
- High risk: SLA-backed enterprise route or route used by multiple customers -> block direct swap, require Red-team assisted rollout (canary + observability hooks + rollback test).

Quick mitigations we can ship fast (low dev effort):
1) Swap guard UI flag: add a modal that shows estimated cost delta (back of envelope) and cache warm-up warning before enabling swap. (Product + Console)
2) Auto-fallback config: per-route policy to auto-fallback to previous model if p99 latency increases by >25% or failure rate increases by >0.5%. (Serving runtime + SRE)
3) KV-cache bucket tagging: persist cache buckets per-model-family so switching between quantization levels within same family shares warm prefixes. (Serving runtime, P0 experiment)
4) Canary slider in Console: simple % slider to route a small fraction of traffic to variant for 10–30 minutes. (Console team)

Cost modeling notes (back-of-envelope numbers):
- Example customer: 30M tokens / month. Swap to cheaper quantized variant predicted -18% token cost, but observed +22% in some cases due to longer generations and tokenization dynamics.
- Net expected saving only if we control output length (via prompt templates or max_tokens limits). Otherwise cost gating is required.

Risk flags and unknowns (things we need data for):
- How often do customers extend prompt templates after swap? (causes length drift) -> add a simple telemetry metric for average generated tokens per route post-swap.
- Regression surface: semantic quality regressions are not reliably captured by latency/err metrics. Need lightweight quality probes (sampled eval prompts) during canary.
- Billing parity: does switching models mid-billing-cycle create customer confusion? Legal/Finance to confirm.

Customer vignettes (short):
- "RetailCo" toggled to lower precision overnight, saw fewer hallucinations but longer completions for multi-turn workflows; they asked to keep quantized variant but with a shorter max_tokens hard cap.
- "AnalyticsCorp" wanted the ability to schedule pre/post market hours model profiles to manage cost; current UI forces manual toggles and lacks rollback transparency.

Implementation recommendations (next 30 days):
- Week 1: Instrumentation tasks — add generated tokens per-route metric and a canary-quality probe scorer (sample 50 prompts/day). (ENG + Observability)
- Week 2: Lightweight Console changes — swap guard modal + canary slider prototype. (Console)
- Week 3–4: Runtime experiments — KV-cache bucket tagging + auto-fallback config prototype on a small fleet. (Serving runtime)
- Parallel: Legal/Finance to draft a short billing FAQ for customers that use mid-cycle swaps. (GTM + Finance)

Decision points for PMs / Execs:
- Do we expose a self-serve mid-window swap control for non-SLA customers with guardrails, or funnel all swaps through CS with Red-team assistance?
- Prioritize KV-cache work (harder runtime change, high long-term ROI) vs. Console UX (lower effort, immediate risk reduction).

Open/questions for reviewers:
- What thresholds should we use for auto-fallback (suggested: p99 +25% and error-rate +0.5%)? Feedback welcome.
- Is the conservative default to block swaps for SLA-backed routes acceptable to Sales? (Liaise with AMs)

Next steps (owner & timeline):
- Maya: draft ticket set for instrumentation and Console modal by 2027-09-17.
- Liam: coordinate with Runtime team for a KV-cache spike feasibility call 2027-09-19.
- Sara: reach out to top 5 customers who requested swaps for short interviews (by 2027-09-22).

Appendix (quick links):
- Linear: INF-4321 (hotswap telemetry)
- Confluence draft: Field Hotswap Playbook (linked above)
- Slack thread: #cs-hotswap-asks (see linked_artifacts)

Notes: this doc is intentionally concise. Use as triage checklist in CS rotations and as input to next sprint refinement. Revisions will follow after the instrumentation results come back.
